Growing Juniper

Launching an Australian health brand into the UK — and discovering that the ‘average visitor’ we were designing for didn’t exist.

On this page

  1. Context
  2. The problem
  3. Finding the split
  4. Testing the theory
  5. Designing for two intents
  6. One decision in detail
  7. The design
  8. Results
  9. What I’d do differently

Context

Eucalyptus is an Australian health company, and this was the launch of its Juniper brand into the UK. Over the course of a year I launched 16 sites. This case study covers the process I used for all of them.

I owned the site design and reported to the Marketing Lead. I worked with an external development team to make sure each site was built as designed, and with the videographers making our video ads, so the material they shot would make sense on the pages people landed on.

The problem

I worked with marketing on a strategy to bring in new customers through Meta and Google, and designed ads for the Meta campaigns. It worked: up to 100,000 new site visitors arrived. But traffic arrived faster than our understanding of it.

We could see the funnel — every visitor loading a page, one in five adding to cart, one in fifty buying — but not who was dropping out, or why. With so few of those 100,000 visitors converting, our cost of acquisition (CAC) was far too high: we were paying to bring people to the site, and most of them left without buying. We were launching into a new market, there was no time for a long research phase, and conversion was the top priority.

Finding the split

To understand who was leaving, I combined two kinds of data: site traffic analytics from Amplitude, and the insights each ad platform gave us about the people clicking. Heatmaps showed what they actually did once they landed.

Put together, the data pointed at a difference we hadn’t expected. It wasn’t about who people were. It was about intent — how ready someone was to buy at the moment they arrived.

Traffic from Meta

Here for the story

  1. Scrolling passively through their feed
  2. An ad’s story catches their interest
  3. They click to learn more
  4. The site has to carry that story on

They convert whenthe story on the site is as compelling as the ad.

Traffic from Google

Here to buy

  1. Types weight loss into Google
  2. Already knows they want to buy something
  3. Clicks through to the site
  4. Wants to check out, now

They convert whennothing stands between them and checkout.

Meta users weren’t looking for us. They were scrolling, and our ads interested them enough to click and find out more. Whether they converted depended on whether the site picked up that story and made it compelling.

Google users had typed ‘weight loss’ into a search bar. They already had high intent and just wanted to buy. For them, the site needed to accommodate that intent and let them get straight to checkout.

Two audiences were arriving on the same pages with opposite needs, and a page built for one was getting in the way of the other. The ‘average visitor’ we’d been designing for didn’t exist. That gave us a theory — not proof. So before redesigning anything, we tested it.

Testing the theory

I tested the theory through incremental A/B tests in Google Optimise. Each test ran on a small percentage of our users, so a wrong idea never cost us much traffic — and a right one could be rolled out with confidence.

After each test we iterated: keeping what worked, dropping what didn’t, and using the result to shape the next test. We tested whole journeys, from the ad someone clicked to the page it sent them to, and weighted testing by risk so the highest-traffic sites went through more rounds.

Test by test, the theory turned into grounded design decisions. Looking back, the tests also gave us something we hadn’t set out to make: a design log of what we’d tried, what we’d learned, and why each decision was made. Working this way also gave senior management the confidence to back the changes.

Designing for two intents

As the tests backed the theory up, I stopped designing one page for everyone and designed for each kind of arrival — starting from the ad that brought someone in.

Traffic from Meta

Do the convincing

People reached these pages from a video ad, so I matched the page to the ad. The imagery, headline and order of content all followed on from what they’d just watched, prioritising the ads I felt were driving the most conversion.

Traffic from Google

Get out of the way

These visitors already knew what they wanted. I cut back on describing the product and gave them a shorter route to checkout.

One decision in detail

The biggest decision the testing led to was to stop sending everyone to the same page. The A/B tests showed how differently people behaved depending on where they came from: their intent was vastly different, so one page could never serve both.

Traffic from Meta

A page that carries the story on

People arriving from a video ad are curious, not ready to buy. They land on the programme page, which picks up the ad’s story and does the convincing: the video, the science, the reviews.

Traffic from Google

The product, up front

People who searched for the treatment by name are ready to buy. They land on the product page, with the medication, doses and supply on the first screen and a short route to checkout.

Search traffic was the clearest proof. It used to land on a beautiful, on-brand page that led with a lifestyle message, and it wasn’t converting: the page was still introducing the brand to people who already knew what they wanted. The product page converted better, and people went through to their cart far more smoothly.

Where a visitor comes from is now one of the first things we consider when designing a page. Each traffic source is directed to a page tailored to its intent, rather than one page trying to serve everyone.

The design

Underneath the testing were the pages and tools themselves. Working within Juniper’s brand, I designed for calm and trust: a warm cream canvas, forest green for anything you act on, lime to draw the eye, and lilac illustration to soften a clinical subject.

The programme pages had a lot of persuading to do, so they lean on warmth: real people, the product in hand, and plain answers to ‘why would this work for me?’.

The product page for search traffic is where testing paid off most, so it got the most care. Everything a ready-to-buy visitor needs sits above the fold: the medication, the dose options, what’s in a month’s supply, the price and one clear next step. The persuasion moves below it, and the FAQs move to the end where people look for them.

On mobile, the eligibility check had to feel like a quick, friendly quiz rather than a medical form. Big inputs, one result in plain words, and a single next step.

The design system behind it

Juniper sat inside a design system shared across four Eucalyptus brands, so every page above is built from the same parts. I worked within it and documented the Juniper layer: a tokenised palette with semantic roles, a two-typeface scale, and components with every size, colour and state defined in auto layout. It meant a test variant could go from idea to live page in days, not weeks, without drifting off-brand.

Results

Conversion improved by an average of 2% across 16 sites, reaching 7% on some. Just as importantly, the optimisation process stuck: both the UK and Australian teams adopted it. It wasn’t a finger-in-the-wind process any more — there was a real understanding of how to build, learn, and serve our customers.

2%Average improvement across 16 sites, with a high of 7%
2 weeksTurnaround for site improvements, down from months
UK + AUSBoth teams adopted the optimisation process

What I’d do differently

I’d have liked to speak to customers. The testing told us which version won, but not always why, and a handful of conversations with people from both channels would have given each hypothesis a firmer starting point.

With four weeks to deliver ahead of a fast-paced launch, there wasn’t room for it this time. It’s the first thing I’d build in on the next project: real conversations running alongside the experiments, so the numbers and the reasons arrive together.
